methods.text: Write the result sentence first, then add only the inputs it needs.
Read the page aloud and cut every line you stumble on.
Check every default value against one real case.
Leave it overnight, then change only what still bothers you.
Name three ways it could be misread and fix each one.
Give it to someone for five minutes and ask them to break it.
Build it twice: once fast, then again from scratch with what you learned.
Remove every word that repeats a heading.

constraints.text: Every input shows its allowed range.
No external files: fonts, scripts, and styles are all inline.

tasks.text: Churn cost calculator: customers lost per month and average yearly value give the revenue lost per year and what keeping one more customer a month would be worth.
Error cost estimator: cases per month, error rate, and cost to fix each error give the monthly cost of errors and the saving if the rate were halved.
Handover gap finder: the steps of a process with the team responsible for each give the points where work changes hands and a count of handovers per case.
Peak load checker: volume by hour of a typical day against staff on duty per hour gives the hours where demand exceeds capacity and by how much.
Quote comparer: up to four quotes with setup cost, monthly cost, and term give the total cost over each term and the lowest cost per year.
Training time estimator: number of staff, training hours each, and hourly cost give the total cost of rolling out a new tool and the weeks to finish.

temperaments.text: Repeats the other side's point before answering.
Asks what would change their mind, then waits.
Writes every claim on the board as it is made.
Goes quiet, then returns with a counter-offer.

guests: historical | Euclid | State a few assumptions, then build everything from them. | died c. 270 BC
historical | Ibn al-Haytham | Trust nothing until an experiment shows it. | died c. 1040
temperaments: Agrees fast, then quietly does it their own way.
Argues the opposite side to test an idea.
methods: Design the error and empty states first.
List the assumptions in the brief and check each one.
Make it work in black and white before adding color.
Take the conventions of a genre and break exactly one.
Write the copy before the layout.
Scope the work to what fits in one day.
constraints: Under 100 words of fixed text on the page.
tasks: Cost-of-inaction calculator: the buyer's current volumes and rates give what the problem costs per month and per year, with each step of the sum shown.
Readiness scorecard: twelve yes-or-no questions give a score out of 100, the three weakest areas, and one next step for each.
Benchmark checker: the buyer's own figures sit next to typical ranges they can edit, with each gap marked ahead, level, or behind.
Leak finder: a funnel of stages with counts gives the stage that loses the most and what fixing half of that loss would be worth.
Time-back calculator: weekly hours on manual tasks and an hourly cost give the hours and money an automated step would return.
Before-and-after map: today's process as a list of steps becomes a side-by-side view marking the steps that could be removed or automated.
